title: Zero Trust
setting: a castle with no inner walls

post.author: u/night_steward_kirsteen
post.title: I'm the night steward at a castle that hosts school trips. This morning's summary from our payroll database says the label printer asked it 214 questions overnight.

blocks.text: I'm Kirsteen, night steward at Ardcullen Castle. We host residential school trips: dormitories, a dining hall, a reception desk. This week a primary school is staying, Monday to Friday.

Every computer, phone and printer here is joined by cables and wifi so they can talk to each other. That's our network. 38 castle devices sit on it. The school's 27 phones and tablets joined it through the guest wifi, which is part of the same network as ours.

Staff pay lives in the payroll database: a program that keeps records and answers questions about them. Each question is called a query. It holds 61 staff: names, home addresses, bank details and pay. Only one program should ever ask it anything: the payroll app on the office computer of Mr Abercairn, our bursar.
Our network meets the internet at one point, the internet link. A firewall stands there: a filter that decides what may come in. That's our outer wall.

Inside, there are no inner doors. When an IT firm built the network in March 2016, it set the payroll database to answer any device inside without asking who it is. A network where everything inside can reach everything is called flat.
The label printer at reception prints luggage and lunch labels. Its maker sends fixes for its software, called software updates. Its last one was installed on Tuesday 11 June 2019.

Every morning at 05:30 the payroll database emails the office a caller summary. A caller is any device that sends it a query. Until today it only ever listed the payroll app. I read the office inbox at the end of my shift, and this morning, Thursday 15 October, it said this. Each line shows the time, the caller, its queries and how many were answered:

00:30-00:31  payroll app      6 queries    6 answered
01:52-03:19  label printer  214 queries  214 answered
Our label printer spent the night asking about our staff.

Someone had taken over the printer; how, we may never know. All 214 queries asked for staff records, and between them the answers could hold all 61. Pupils' details weren't there: bookings live with an online booking service outside the castle.

diagram.aria: My sketch of last night's network. Top row: the firewall at the internet link; the label printer, last updated on 11 June 2019, sending 214 queries to the payroll database; and the payroll database, holding 61 staff records and answering anyone inside. Bottom row: the guest wifi with the school's 27 devices, which can reach payroll; 34 more castle devices, which can reach payroll; and the payroll app, whose 6 queries came at 00:30. A note says all 64 devices inside were answered alike.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from my notes on Thursday 15 October 2026. Our 38 castle devices: 2 reception computers, the label printer, 3 booking computers, the payroll computer that runs the payroll app, the payroll database, 16 staff laptops, 4 kitchen tablets, 9 door cameras and the guest wifi box. With the school's 27, 64 devices could reach the payroll database, and it answered every one alike. Overnight only two asked: the payroll app, 6 queries at 00:30, and the label printer, 214 between 01:52 and 03:19.

blocks.text: At 05:41 I unplugged the printer and rang Mr Abercairn. He is telling the 61 staff today. The next school arrives on Monday 19 October, and the owners want a change before then. Their first thought is a new printer. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Look at your own numbers before you choose, Kirsteen. Last night, how many devices could reach the payroll database, and how many would it answer? Which side is the printer on, the guests' or the staff's? How many devices come through your gate each week that the IT firm has never seen? And read the caller summary once more: before it answered, what did the database know about the printer, apart from where it sat?

replies.author: u/night_steward_kirsteen
replies.text: 64 could reach it: 37 castle devices and the school's 27. It would answer all 64 alike. The printer is on the staff side, a cable away from the bursar's office. Through the gate: a new school every week, 27 devices this week, and 16 staff laptops that go home every evening. The database knew nothing about the printer except that it was inside.

comments.author: u/strong_gate_fabienne
comments.text: A good outer wall is enough. Nothing bad gets inside the castle if the gate is strong. Whatever took over your printer came in from the internet, so put a stronger firewall at the internet link, one that inspects everything coming in, and keep the inside simple. Inner doors only slow your own staff down.

replies.author: u/night_steward_kirsteen
replies.text: The owners like this one. One box at the link, and nothing changes for the staff.

comments.author: u/trip_leader_moncrieff
comments.text: I lead school trips most terms. The first thing our school's IT team asks any centre is whether pupils' tablets share a network with the office. Put guests and school groups on their own wifi, kept apart from your systems. It's cheap, and parents ask about it.

reply.prompt: The next school arrives on Monday 19 October. What should Ardcullen Castle change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Replace the old label printer with a new one that gets every software update.
options.part2: On Friday 16 October the owners bought a new label printer that installs its own updates. In the sim, replaying the night with it, the printer's line in the caller summary is empty. Nothing else moves: 64 devices can still reach payroll, and it still answers all 64, because it still asks nobody who they are. 9 of them are the door cameras, last updated on Tuesday 17 May 2022. Mr Abercairn asked the IT firm which other devices nobody updates. They had no list.
options.senior: Replacing a device nobody updated is right, and keeping a list of every device and its updates is better. But it fixes this printer, not the design that made it dangerous. Payroll still trusts anything inside, so the next forgotten camera, laptop or visitor's tablet that is taken over can ask the same questions. Fix the reason one device could read every pay record: make the record holder check identity, and limit who can reach it.

options.text: Put guests and school groups on their own wifi, kept apart from the castle's systems.
options.verdict: A real wall, in the wrong place
options.part2: The IT firm gave the guest wifi a network of its own on Saturday 17 October. In the sim the school's 27 devices and the guest wifi box leave the grid: 36 devices can reach payroll, not 64, and 0 of them the school's. That's a real inner wall: pupils' tablets can no longer reach any castle system, and parents were glad to hear it. But replaying the night, the label printer still sits on the staff side, beside payroll: 214 queries, 214 answered, and the answers could hold all 61 staff records.
options.senior: Splitting guests off is network segmentation, and it is worth doing for any network that strangers join. But it draws one inner wall, between guests and staff, and leaves the staff side flat: the printer, the cameras and 16 laptops still sit beside payroll, and payroll still answers whatever is inside. Segment by role, and still make the most valuable system check every caller, because the next problem may start on the staff side.

options.text: Put a stronger firewall at the castle's internet link, so nobody gets in to begin with.
options.part2: On Friday 16 October the IT firm fitted a stronger firewall at the internet link. In the sim the grid doesn't change: 64 devices can reach payroll, and it answers all 64. Replaying the night, the printer's 214 queries start inside the castle and never cross the firewall: 214 answered, and the answers could hold all 61 staff records. And the gate isn't the only way in: this week 27 school devices came in someone's bag, and 16 staff laptops go home and come back every day.
options.senior: An outer firewall is worth having, and it only sees traffic that crosses the internet link. Devices come inside in other ways, and once one is inside and taken over, a flat network gives it everything. NIST's zero trust guidance says it plainly: network location alone does not imply trust. Keep the outer wall, and stop treating inside as proof of anything.

options.text: Make payroll check who every caller is, and answer only the payroll app itself.
options.part2: Mr Abercairn signed the change on Saturday 17 October, and the IT firm made it. The castle now issues its own certificates, signed ID files, to its own machines. The payroll app and the payroll database each got one. Before any question, each side shows its certificate and proves it holds the matching private key, and each checks the other's: mutual TLS. Payroll then answers only the certificate named for the payroll app. In the sim, replaying the night: 64 devices can still reach payroll, but it answers 1. The app's 6 queries at 00:30 are answered; the printer's 214 are refused, and the answers hold 0 staff records. Out-of-date devices payroll would answer: 0, not 10. The guest wifi and the cameras are next on the list.
options.senior: Put the check where the valuable thing lives. When payroll asks every caller to prove who it is, on every request, and answers only the one caller that needs it, a device taken over anywhere inside gets nothing, wherever it sits and however it got in. Mutual TLS gives that proof between machines: both sides show a certificate and prove they hold its key. Then add inner walls by role, keep devices updated, and watch the caller summary, because each layer catches what another misses.

sim.title: Who can reach payroll, and who does it answer?

The night: at 00:30 the payroll app sends 6 queries; from 01:52 to 03:19 the label printer, already taken over, a given event, sends 214 queries for staff records; at 05:30 the caller summary goes to the office. Devices are only labels here. Set the layout, payroll's rule, the outer firewall and the printer, read who can reach payroll and who it would answer, then play the night.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play the night as built: 64 devices can reach payroll, it answers all 64, and the printer's 214 queries are all answered. Replace the printer: no queries from it, but payroll still answers 64, 9 of them out-of-date cameras. Split off the guest wifi: 36 can reach payroll, 0 school devices, and the printer's 214 are still answered. Try the stronger firewall: nothing inside changes. Set payroll to answer only the payroll app: it answers 1, the app's 6 queries pass, and the printer's 214 are refused.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the record broke the outer wall. A device already inside, the old label printer, asked the payroll database 214 questions, and the database answered because the printer was inside. Make the database check who every caller is, on every request, and answer only the payroll app; then add inner walls by role.

steps.title: What happened: trust by location.
steps.text: Ardcullen's network is flat: once a device is inside, it can reach everything, and the payroll database answered any device inside. Guarding only the edge and trusting everything within is called perimeter security. Using one device that has been taken over to reach other systems on the same network is called lateral movement, and it works because on a flat network those systems answer whatever is inside. Here is what went wrong, in order. First, the printer went years without a software update. Second, it sat on the same network as payroll. Third, payroll asked no caller who it was. Each step alone is common; together they let one forgotten printer reach every pay record.

steps.title: Inner walls: network segmentation.
steps.text: Network segmentation splits a network into groups by role, with inner walls between them. Do it in steps. First, list every device and what it does: front desk, office, staff, building, guests. Second, write down which group needs to reach which system: only the payroll computer needs payroll. Third, allow those paths and block every other one by default. Fourth, review the list whenever a device arrives. In a cloud the same idea is a VPC, short for virtual private cloud: a private network you define, split into subnets, with security groups as a doorkeeper on each resource. What goes wrong: walls drawn once and never reviewed, and a group so broad that the wrong devices share it.

steps.title: Identity on every request.
steps.text: A wall decides who can knock; identity decides who gets an answer. With identity on every request, each caller proves who it is every time it asks, wherever it sits, and the system then decides whether that caller may have this answer. In steps: first, every program that should call payroll gets its own identity; second, every request carries proof of it; third, payroll checks the proof; fourth, payroll answers only the identities on its list, with the least they need. What goes wrong: one identity shared by many machines, or proof that never expires, so a copy works for ever.

steps.title: Mutual TLS, step by step.
steps.text: TLS, the padlock's protective layer, normally has only the server prove who it is with a certificate, a signed ID file. Mutual TLS asks both sides. First, the payroll app connects and the database shows its certificate and proves it holds the matching private key. Second, the app checks that certificate was signed by the castle's own certificate authority and names the payroll database. Third, the database asks for the app's certificate, and the app shows it and proves it holds its key. Fourth, the database checks the signature and the name, payroll app, and only then reads the query. The printer has no such certificate, so it stops at the third step. What goes wrong: a private key copied to another machine, certificates that never expire, and a check that accepts any certificate the castle signed rather than the one name it expects.

steps.title: Zero trust: inside proves nothing.
steps.text: Zero trust puts these together: no trust is granted for being on a network, every request is checked for identity and need, and access is the least that does the job. NIST SP 800-207 states it as tenets: all communication is secured regardless of network location, and access is granted per session after the requester is evaluated. It does not mean removing walls or firewalls. It means no wall is the reason to answer. What goes wrong: buying a product called zero trust and leaving one database that still answers anything inside.

diagram.aria: Mutual TLS between the payroll app and the payroll database, and the label printer refused. The app says hello. The database shows its certificate and proof; the app checks it is castle-signed and named payroll database. The database asks for the app's certificate; the app shows it with proof; the database checks it is castle-signed and named payroll app, which is allowed. The app sends its query at 00:30 and it is answered. The label printer says hello at 01:52; the database asks for its certificate. Outcome: no certificate, 214 of 214 refused.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the night of 14 to 15 October. Both the payroll app and the payroll database show a certificate signed by the castle and prove they hold its key, and the database answers only the name payroll app. The label printer can still knock, but it has no certificate, so all 214 of its queries are refused before a single answer.

fix.title: The fix: payroll checks every caller, every time, and answers only the payroll app; then inner walls by role
fix.text: Set up a certificate authority for the castle's own machines. Give the payroll app and the payroll database each a certificate, with its private key kept on that machine and never copied, and short enough to expire within weeks and renew by itself. Turn on mutual TLS at the database, and answer only the certificate named for the payroll app, with only the records it needs. Then draw inner walls by role: front desk, office, staff, building and guests, where only the payroll computer can reach payroll and the guest wifi reaches nothing of the castle's. Keep a list of every device with its last update, and replace or wall off what can't be updated. Keep the outer firewall. Keep the caller summary, and have it alert someone the moment a caller it doesn't know appears, rather than at 05:30.

limits: Mutual TLS proves a caller holds a key, not which machine it is or who is at it. If the payroll app's private key is copied to another machine, that machine is the payroll app as far as the database can tell.

If the payroll computer itself is taken over, it holds the right certificate and passes every check. Inner walls, the least access per caller and a caller summary that alerts on odd hours still matter.
None of this tells the 61 staff what was read. The castle can only say what the answers could have held, and must treat it as read.

explain.seniorTake: A perimeter is one wall, and a wall only matters at the moment something crosses it. Devices arrive inside in bags, on laptops that go home, and as old machines nobody updates, so plan as if something inside is already taken over. Put the strongest check on the systems that matter most: every caller proves its identity on every request, with mutual TLS between machines, and gets only the least it needs. Then draw inner walls by role, so that a taken-over device reaches little even before identity is checked, and keep a list of every device and its updates. Zero trust is not a product or the removal of firewalls; it is the rule that being inside proves nothing. Watch for what it costs: certificates to issue, renew and keep on one machine, and walls to review as devices change.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-207, 2020: no trust for location
realWorld.text: NIST's Zero Trust Architecture says in its abstract: "Zero trust assumes there is no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location (i.e., local area networks versus the internet) or based on asset ownership (enterprise or personally owned)." Its introduction adds: "Perimeter-based network security has also been shown to be insufficient since once attackers breach the perimeter, further lateral movement is unhindered."

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-207: the tenets
realWorld.text: Tenet 2: "All communication is secured regardless of network location. Network location alone does not imply trust." It goes on: "trust should not be automatically granted based on the device being on enterprise network infrastructure." Tenet 3: "Access to individual enterprise resources is granted on a per-session basis. Trust in the requester is evaluated before the access is granted." And among its assumptions: "The entire enterprise private network is not considered an implicit trust zone."

realWorld.title: Google BeyondCorp, 2014: removing the trusted intranet
realWorld.text: Rory Ward and Betsy Beyer's paper in ;login: begins: "Virtually every company today uses firewalls to enforce perimeter security." The model is a problem "because, when that perimeter is breached," and then "an attacker has relatively easy access to a company's privileged intranet." Google's answer: "We are removing the requirement for a privileged intranet and moving our corporate applications to the Internet."

realWorld.title: Equifax, 2017: databases not segmented
realWorld.text: The US Government Accountability Office's report GAO-18-559 (August 2018) lists segmentation among the factors Equifax identified: "Because individual databases were not isolated or “segmented” from each other, the attackers were able to access additional databases beyond the ones related to the online dispute portal, according to Equifax officials." It counts access reaching "beyond the 3 databases associated with the online dispute portal, to include an additional 48 unrelated databases." Its footnote: "Segmentation allows an organization to logically separate applications based on their sensitivity level or to keep unrelated applications from communicating with each other."

realWorld.title: TLS 1.3: the client side is optional
realWorld.text: RFC 8446 says: "Authentication: The server side of the channel is always authenticated; the client side is optionally authenticated." Mutual TLS is the choice to turn that optional client side on, so the server learns who is calling as well.

realWorld.title: Amazon VPC: a private network you define
realWorld.text: Amazon's documentation: "With Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), you can launch AWS resources in a logically isolated virtual network that you've defined." Inside it, subnets group resources, much as the castle could group devices by role.

realWorld.title: AWS security groups: a doorkeeper per resource
realWorld.text: For the inner walls, the same guide says: "A security group controls the traffic that is allowed to reach and leave the resources that it is associated with." A database's security group can accept traffic only from the application's own group, which is segmentation by role in a cloud.

asked: What does zero trust mean in practice?
How would you segment a cloud network?
interview.answer: Zero trust means no request is trusted because of where it comes from. Being on the office network or inside the cloud network proves nothing; every caller proves who it is on every request, the system checks whether that caller may do this, and it gets the least it needs. In practice I start with the systems that matter most, such as the database with customer or pay records, and make them check identity on every call. Between machines I'd use mutual TLS. In ordinary TLS only the server shows a certificate. In mutual TLS, first the server shows its certificate and proves it holds the private key; the client checks the signature, from our own certificate authority, and the name. Then the server asks for the client's certificate, the client shows it and proves it holds its key, and the server checks the signature and that the name is one it allows. Only then does it read the request. I'd keep keys on the machine, make certificates short-lived and renew them automatically, and allow names, not any certificate we signed. For a cloud network, I'd use a VPC, a private network we define, split into subnets by role, with the database in a private subnet that has no route from the internet. Security groups act as a doorkeeper on each resource: the database accepts traffic only from the application's security group, the application only from the load balancer's. Then I'd review those rules when services change, log who calls what, and alert on callers that aren't expected. Segmentation limits who can knock; identity decides who gets an answer, and I want both. I'd close with the castle: a label printer nobody updated asked payroll 214 questions and got 214 answers, because inside was treated as proof.

atWork: Find the places where being inside your network is the reason a system answers. A common pattern is an office or cloud network where every machine can reach the main database, and the database accepts any connection from inside with one shared login. For each valuable system, ask: which callers can reach it, which does it answer, and how does it know who each one is? Then fix it in order. First, make the system check identity on every request: mutual TLS or a per-service identity between machines, one identity per caller, keys that stay on their machine, certificates that expire and renew. Second, draw inner walls by role: in AWS, a VPC with private subnets for databases and security groups that accept traffic only from the application's own security group. Third, keep a list of every device and its updates, and log and alert on callers you don't expect. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, this is Annex A 8.20 (networks security) and A.8.22 (segregation of networks); if your SOC 2 report is in scope, CC6.6 (logical access security measures against threats from sources outside system boundaries) applies; and if card payments run on the same network, PCI DSS expects that network to be segmented from the systems that handle card data, or all of it falls in scope. A flat network with a database that trusts location is a finding an auditor is likely to raise, so design the inner walls and the identity checks in from the first diagram rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company runs its apps in one private cloud network. Every server in it can reach the customer database, which accepts any connection from inside with one shared login. Last month a contractor added a test machine there that nobody updates. A review asks what you would change. What do you say?

keyIdeas.idea: Being inside the network should prove nothing; the database should make every caller prove who it is on every request
Give each service its own identity, such as mutual TLS certificates, and have the database answer only the app that needs it
Segment the network: only the app's servers can reach the database, using private subnets and security groups

recall.model: Being inside the network should prove nothing, so I'd start at the database rather than the edge. Replace the one shared login with an identity per service: mutual TLS, where the app and the database each show a certificate and prove they hold its key, so the database answers only the app that needs it and checks that on every request. Keep keys on their machines and certificates short-lived. Then segment: put the database in a private subnet with a security group that accepts traffic only from the app's own security group, so the contractor's test machine can't even reach it. Finally, update or remove the test machine, keep a list of every machine, and alert on callers the database doesn't expect.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with the network still flat, which change gets the label printer's queries refused?
options: A new label printer that gets every update
Guests and school groups on their own wifi
A stronger firewall at the internet link
recall.why: Only payroll's new rule changes who gets an answer: it asks every caller for a certificate and answers only the payroll app, so the printer's 214 are refused. The guest wifi split and the firewall leave the printer beside payroll and answered; a new printer just means a different device is the one payroll would trust.

recall.prompt: What does mutual TLS add to ordinary TLS?
options: The client also shows a certificate and proves it holds the key
The connection is scrambled so others can't read it
The server shows a certificate signed by an authority
The firewall checks every message at the edge
recall.why: Ordinary TLS already scrambles the connection and has the server prove who it is. Mutual TLS turns on the optional client side, so the server learns which caller it is talking to and can refuse any it doesn't allow.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked what zero trust means in practice, beyond the slogan. What do you say?

keyIdeas.idea: No trust is granted because of where a request comes from: being inside the network proves nothing
Every request is checked for identity and permission, each time
Each caller gets the least access it needs, and segmentation limits what a taken-over device can reach

recall.model: Zero trust means no request is trusted because of its network location: being inside the office or cloud network proves nothing, because devices get taken over and arrive inside in many ways. Every request is checked, each time, for who the caller is and whether it may do this, with mutual TLS or similar identity between machines and strong sign-in for people. Each caller gets least privilege, only what it needs, and inner walls by role limit what a taken-over device can reach even before identity is checked. It doesn't mean throwing away firewalls; it means no wall is the reason to answer.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Payroll's new rule held all winter: every caller summary listed only the payroll app. In December Mr Abercairn got a laptop so he could run payroll from home too, over a link the IT firm set up, and to save a day the firm put a copy of the payroll app's certificate and its private key on it. On Monday 11 January 2027 the laptop went missing from his car. On Tuesday 12 January the 05:30 summary showed 88 queries from the payroll app between 02:04 and 02:40, all answered, while the payroll computer was switched off.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Mutual TLS was on, so why did payroll answer, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The private key was copied, so whoever holds the copy is the payroll app as far as the database can tell; the check proves the key, not the machine
Revoke that certificate now and issue one per device, with the key kept on the device and never copied
Check more than the certificate: short-lived certificates, the device, and alerts on unexpected times

coldCase.model: Mutual TLS proves the caller holds the payroll app's private key, not which machine it is. The firm copied the key onto the laptop, so whoever has the laptop holds the same certificate and the same key, and to the database it is the payroll app. Revoke that certificate today, so the database stops accepting it, and issue a new one per device: one for the payroll computer, another for the laptop, each with its key kept in the device's own hardware, where it can't be copied. Let payroll allow each name separately, so a lost laptop can be cut off alone. Make certificates short-lived so a stolen one expires soon, check the device as well as the key, and have the caller summary alert someone at once when queries come at odd hours, not at 05:30.
